summary: CryoZip is a cryogenic syndrome compression framework for quantum error correction that achieves up to $48\times$ compression across surface, BB, and color codes by encoding distances between consecutive active syndromes followed by Huffman encoding. Implemented in 22 nm FDSOI cryo-CMOS and evaluated at 4 K, CryoZip cooperates with lightweight cryogenic predecoders to deliver over $14{,}238\times$ bandwidth reduction and up to $42\times$ energy savings while meeting strict $100$ ns latency constraints per syndrome round.
motivation: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing faces a critical bottleneck: cryogenic dilution refrigerators have only $\sim 1.5$ W cooling power at 4 K, yet QEC syndrome transmission from qubits to room-temperature decoders dominates this budget at 0.92 $\mu$W per bit, limiting support to only $\sim 1000$ logical qubits far below the $10^5$–$10^6$ needed for practical FTQC.
method: CryoZip compresses sparse syndrome vectors via a Sparse Distance (SD) algorithm that encodes gaps between active syndromes, followed by Huffman entropy coding with a static offline-generated codebook. A pipelined sliding-window hardware design in 22 nm FDSOI processes one syndrome round per $1\,\mu$s measurement cycle within a $100$ ns latency budget, reducing area and power overhead by up to $12.2\times$ and $8.7\times$ compared to full-vector processing.
result: CryoZip achieves $48.3\times$ compression on the surface code ($d=17$, $p=0.1\times 10^{-4}$) and maintains $5.35\times$ in practical regimes ($d=21$, $p=10^{-3}$), delivering $1.8\times$ higher compression than state-of-the-art methods; when paired with a cryogenic predecoder, bandwidth reduction exceeds $14{,}238\times$ while energy savings reach $42\times$ accounting for realistic QECi packet overhead.
